wine.name: La Faraona
wine.sites: A tiny plot high on the slopes above Corullón, near the upper limit of the vine in Bierzo, facing south east on slate, its pitch so steep that every task is done by hand.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented in an oak vat with a share of whole bunches that the vintage decides, then left long on its skins. It is aged in a mix of barrels and larger casks, few of them new, for a time that has ranged from under a year to a year and a half, and bottled without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Violet and rose petal over wild raspberry, red cherry and wet slate, with a hint of black pepper and dried herbs; pale for its depth, taut and fresh, with fine, close grained tannin and a long, stony finish.
wine.ageing: Taut and closed when young, it gains perfume with several years in bottle and is built to keep well beyond a decade in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead to open its perfume; a large Burgundy glass.

records.table: La Faraona is the high single plot at the head of Descendientes de J. Palacios's range at Corullón: old Mencía on slate, fermented with some whole bunches and aged in used wood. Pale, perfumed and taut, it wants a Burgundy glass and a little air.
records.story: The house is named for the descendants of J. Palacios, patriarch of a family of wine growers in Rioja. In 1999 one of his sons, already making wine in Priorat, and that son's nephew came to Bierzo in search of old Mencía on ground hard to reach and slow to yield, and settled on the steep slate around Corullón, on the western edge of the basin. They made their first wine that year. In 2001 they chose to bottle a few plots on their own, and one of them, high near the upper limit of the vine above the village, became La Faraona. Around it the house built a ladder in the Burgundian manner: Pétalos del Bierzo as the regional wine, Villa de Corullón from the village and named sites such as Moncerbal and Las Lamas above it, with the vines farmed biodynamically. The denomination later wrote such a ladder into its own rules, and when it did the Consejo foresaw the first Viña Clasificada wines no earlier than 2025 and the first Gran Viña Clasificada no earlier than 2030. La Faraona shows a sommelier what one high plot of old Mencía can give: perfume and tension rather than weight.

report: Searches for this record: 10 of the group's share of 35, beside three the group shared on the denomination's rules; one fetch was tried (rarewineco.com, refused) and never retried, so the importer's article and sheet were read through search alone, and the south east aspect on slate is borne out by a second merchant's sheet (Vino.com, morning sun at 950 metres).

The plan's note is answered by leaving classification empty: no source read gives La Faraona a rank of the denomination's ladder, one merchant's page calls it a Gran Vinya Classificada (Priorat's Catalan term) and one news item of 2026 a viña clasificada, while the Consejo's own page foresaw the first Viña Clasificada wines no earlier than 2025 and the first Gran Viña Clasificada no earlier than 2030.

Founded is the library's 1999 and the first wine of 1999 rests on the importer's sheet and article; one importer's sheet gives the company as established in 1998, and the first separate bottling of La Faraona in 2001 rests on the importer's article and Spanish Wine Lover.

The plot's altitude is about 855 metres on the importer's sheet, more than 800, 900 and 950 in merchants' listings and about 975 or nearly 1,000 in others, so the record says near the upper limit of the vine; the paraje is named El Fierro, El Ferro and El Ferrol in three listings and one sheet places it on a tectonic fault, so neither the name nor the fault is given.

The ageing is nine to ten months in barrel for the 2019 (Berry Bros.), twelve in foudre and barrique for the 2018, six and a half in one shop's sheet and fifteen to eighteen months for the house's wines above Pétalos in an older Spanish Wine Lover article, hence the range; the whole bunch share is 10 to 50 per cent by vintage (Spanish Wine Lover) and over 30 per cent on the importer's sheet, with 0 to 30 per cent new wood and maceration of 45 to 90 days in one oak vat.

Left out for want of a second source tied to a listed page: the patriarch's death in 2000 (in several accounts read through search), the origin of the name La Faraona, the vines' age (seventy and more, and eighty two, in two listings) and any horses or mules in the vineyards.
The library's w-la-faraona calls the wine the summit of Bierzo's classified ladder; that reads true of the house's own ladder, but no source read gives it a rank of the denomination's.
Living names met, none in the fragment: the son and the nephew who founded the house (both on people.json); the patriarch is described, not named, since his dates were not found in two sources.

wine.name: Ultreia Saint Jacques
wine.grapes: Mencía, all or almost all of it, from old vines.
wine.sites: The family's old vineyards around Valtuille de Abajo, several plots picked each year, crossed by the pilgrims' road to Santiago.
wine.making: Fermented with whole bunches, stems and all, and left long on its skins; the wine is then aged in old wood, used barrels and large truncated cone vats among it, before it is bottled.
wine.glass: Red cherry, wild strawberry and blood orange over crushed slate, with a green, peppery lift from the stems and a breath of sea air; light to medium in body, juicy and fresh, with fine, slightly grainy tannin.
wine.ageing: Lively and open on release, it drinks well over its first several years and gains savoury notes of dried cherry and leaf with a few more.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius, a little cool to keep it fresh; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

records.table: Ultreia Saint Jacques is the Raúl Pérez house's Mencía from old family vines at Valtuille de Abajo, where the pilgrims' road crosses the vineyards. Made with whole bunches and aged in old wood, it is fresh, juicy and lightly peppery; pour it a little cool.
records.story: Bierzo was recognised as a denomination in 1989, and much of its revival in the years after came from growers raised among its old vines. The grower behind this house comes from a family of Valtuille de Abajo and learnt his trade at its bodega before going his own way. In 2003, or 2004 by some accounts, he began to bottle under his own name and called the range Ultreia, the Latin greeting pilgrims give one another on the road to Santiago, read as go further. That road runs through the vineyards of the village, and Saint Jacques, the apostle at its end in French, names the Mencía drawn from the family's old vines there, picked from several plots each year. The house works with whole bunches, long macerations, old wood and little sulphur, after perfume and freshness rather than weight. From Bierzo the grower carried the same ways west into Galicia, to Ribeira Sacra and Rías Baixas, so that the house's name is met across the Atlantic north west. Ultreia Saint Jacques is its wide release: the old Mencía of Valtuille, fragrant and lively, made for the table rather than the cellar.

report: Searches for this record: 5 of the group's share of 35, one of them restricted to four guessed house domains and empty; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: Bodeboca, Vinissimus and Mentta print Ultreia Saint Jacques and the importer Skurnik prints Ultreia St. Jacques, both with Bierzo; the record keeps the plan's Saint Jacques, and the label term means only what the words mean, since no label image was read.
Founded is left empty: Spanish Wine Lover gives 2003 for the grower's own range and Winetraveler's sources and others 2004, so the story gives both.

The making rests on Bodeboca's sheet (stems kept, a long maceration, about fourteen months in used barrels and truncated cone vats) and Clos des Millésimes (whole stems in open oak vats, not listed because its address carries a run of hyphens); the fourteen months, the open vats and Bodeboca's clay and limestone soil are left out as single sourced.

The grapes are given as all or almost all Mencía because Bodeboca gives 100 per cent for 2022 and another account a little Trousseau and Tintorera from a plot of 1936; the vineyard dates (1910, 1936, more than 130 years) disagree and are left out.

The library's p-raul-perez calls the grower the consultant behind much of the Atlantic revival; no source read calls him a consultant, so the record speaks of the house's own work in Ribeira Sacra and Rías Baixas (the library's Monterrei and one source's Tierra de León are left out).

wine.name: Valtuille Cepas Centenarias
wine.grapes: Mencía, the great majority, with a little Garnacha Tintorera and Bastardo growing among it in the old field blend.
wine.sites: The family's old vineyards around Valtuille de Abajo, Mencía more than a century old; in its later vintages the wine has come from a single plot.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented, the wine is aged for about a year in used French oak barrels of different sizes, which let it breathe slowly without tasting of wood, and it is bottled without fining or filtering.
wine.glass: Ripe red and black cherry, blueberry and violet over liquorice, graphite and a savoury, peppery edge; medium to full in body and fresh, with firm, fine tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Firm for its first few years, it opens with time in bottle and keeps well for a decade or more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle an hour ahead; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Castro Ventosa is the family bodega of Valtuille de Abajo, and Valtuille Cepas Centenarias its Mencía from vines more than a century old. Aged about a year in used French oak, it is deep and savoury yet fresh, a red to decant an hour ahead.
records.story: The bodega takes its name from Castro Ventosa, the walled hill site between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo, long linked with Bergidum Flavium, the Roman town from which Bierzo is held to take its name; the family's cellar stands at the foot of its western slope. By the house's account the family has grown vines at Valtuille de Abajo since 1752, on plots that became part of the estate, across nine generations. For most of that time it sold its wine in bulk. It bottled its first estate wines in 1989, and in 1991 gave the bodega the name of the hill. Valtuille Cepas Centenarias followed with the 1999 vintage, drawn from the family's Mencía of a century and more, with a little Garnacha Tintorera and Bastardo among them, as the old growers planted. In 2017, as the denomination prepared its ladder of village and site wines, the house added a village wine named for Valtuille, and wines of named sites of the village sit above it. For Cepas Centenarias the cellar keeps to used French barrels, so that the old vines speak rather than the wood. For a sommelier, Cepas Centenarias shows what a century of vine age gives Mencía: depth and calm without heaviness.

report: Searches for this record: 7 of the group's share of 35, one restricted to the house's domain and the region's tourism portal; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: the house's own pages give the family's vines at Valtuille since 1752 across nine generations, the cellar at the foot of the western slope of the Roman site that gives it its name, Cepas Centenarias made since 1999 and the village wine Castro Ventosa Valtuille of 2017; the century old vines are given by the house's importers (Indigo Wine, Kensington) and Bodeboca.

Founded is left empty: the family dates its vines to 1752 and its first estate bottling to 1989, and the bodega took its name in 1991 (Enterwine, with a wiki entry and a second listing read through search), so no single year founds the house; one listing gives 1999, the year of Cepas Centenarias.

The field blend rests on Bodeboca's sheet for 2022 (Alicante Bouschet, which is Garnacha Tintorera, and Bastardo) and Grand Cru Wijnen's for 2023 (a single plot at Mata Los Pardos with a little Trousseau, which is Bastardo); the single plot also rests on Bodeboca's 2021 sheet, and the plot's name is left out as single sourced.

About a year in used French barrels rests on Bodeboca (twelve months, 225 and 500 litres), Vinos Cutanda and Private Cellar (eleven months) and Gourmet Hunters (twelve, unfined and unfiltered); the fermentation in a 5,000 litre foudre with native yeasts and sixty days on the skins is Bodeboca's for one vintage and is left out.

The plan's sandy valley floor is not borne out for this wine: one listing gives its soil as mostly clay, another the Villegas plot as sandy, so no soil is given; ungrafted vines rest on one importer and are left out.

The bond with Bergidum Flavium is hedged because the University of Salamanca's study says the hill has always been linked with the Roman town while the town's exact site is disputed (Castro Ventosa or La Edrada at Cacabelos); the Templar castle at Ponferrada in a question's explanation rests on general knowledge, not a listed source.

Living names met, for people.json: the grower who founded the Ultreia house and his nephew, the winemaker, of the family (see raul-perez), and the founder of another Valtuille bodega met on the tourism portal (Marcos García Alba); the grandmother named in the bodega's first name of 1989 is not named for want of dates.

wine.name: Cepas Viejas
wine.grapes: Mencía alone, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: Old bush vines of eighty years and more on decomposed slate, up to about 700 metres, from plots in several parts of the denomination, in some vintages around the hill of Castro Ventosa.
wine.making: Made as an oak aged red: after fermentation the wine spends some nine to ten months in oak barrels and then rests for many months in bottle before the house releases it, the Mencía meant to lead rather than the wood.
wine.glass: Black cherry, blackberry and ripe plum over violet, liquorice and toast from the barrel, with a savoury, slaty edge; medium to full in body, ripe and smooth, with fresh acidity and rounded tannin.
wine.ageing: Ready to drink when it is released, it keeps its fruit for several years and gains savoury depth with a few more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 16 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant half an hour ahead for its aroma; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Cepas Viejas is the red that launched Dominio de Tares in Bierzo Alto: Mencía from old bush vines on slate, aged some ten months in oak. Dark fruited, smooth and lightly toasted, it shows the riper, oak aged face of the grape.
records.story: Dominio de Tares was born in 2000 at San Román de Bembibre, in Bierzo Alto on the eastern side of the basin, as a house set on recovering old vineyards. Its founders, by the house's account, searched the denomination for sites on very different soils. Cepas Viejas was its first wine: a modern red, aged in oak, in which Mencía was meant to stand at the centre, made from bush vines of eighty years and more on decomposed slate. Beside it the house made a Godello fermented in barrel, and it took part in reviving two old reds of the north west, Prieto Picudo of León and Estaladiña of Bierzo. The denomination itself worked from 2015 on new rules that the Ministry ratified in 2019, adding Estaladiña and Merenzao to its grapes and a ladder of village, site and classified vineyard wines. In time the house gave the name Cepas Viejas to its barrel fermented Godello as well, so that a red and a white share it. For a sommelier, Cepas Viejas stands for the Bierzo of the early 2000s: ripe Mencía from old vines, shaped by oak.

Dominio de Tares stands in Bierzo Alto, around Bembibre in the east of the basin, not in the western villages of Corullón or Valtuille.

report: Searches for this record: 4 of the group's share of 35, two restricted to the house's own domains; no fetch tried for this house.

The plan's note is answered: the house's own pages give 2000 for its birth (with Spanish Wine Lover and Cellar Tours), Cepas Viejas as its first wine, Mencía alone, vines of more than eighty five years up to 700 metres on decomposed slate and, for one vintage, bush vines of more than eighty years around the Castro Bergidum, which is Castro Ventosa; the record says eighty years and more because the figure grows each year.

The Godello of the same name is kept apart in a trap and in others: the house's shop and its sheet for 2023 give wild yeasts, 500 litre barrels and about six months on the lees in French oak; the year of the renaming (2024 in the plan, a Cepas Viejas Godello 2023 sheet uploaded in 2024) is left out.

The time in oak is ten months on the house's shop and its note on the 2022, nine in one shop's listing and nine for the 2011 in the house's own news, with French and American barrels for that vintage; the American share and the eighteen months in bottle of one vintage are left out, and the record says many months in bottle.

Left out for want of a second source: the group of friends who founded the house (one retailer quoting the house), the old vineyards of forty to ninety years in three zones, the growers it buys from in Valtuille de Abajo and Villadecanes (Spanish Wine Lover alone), its claim to have pioneered aged Mencía and barrel fermented Godello, and the meaning of the name Tares; the closing line is the author's reading of the house's own words for the checker to test.
The region's producers line (one of the first serious barrel fermented Godellos) is not borne out by two sources and is not repeated; the plan's slate and clay is the house's decomposed slate.
Living names met, none in the fragment: a person interviewed for the house on Onda Madrid (Rafael Somonte, role not read), for people.json as a precaution.

wine.sites: Old vines on the clay slopes near the cellar at Pieros, on the pilgrims' road between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo, farmed as many small plots.
wine.making: The grapes come from the house's own small plots near the cellar at Pieros and are fermented there; the wine is then aged for about a year in French oak barrels before bottling, by the house's own sheet.
wine.glass: Ripe red cherry, raspberry and blackberry over violet, liquorice and a hint of toast, with a peppery, herb edge; round and supple, with fresh acidity and soft, ripe tannin.
wine.ageing: Generous on release, it drinks well over its first five years or so and gains savoury notes with a few more.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; it needs no decanting, though a few minutes of air help; a large red wine glass.

records.table: Losada is the namesake Mencía of Losada Vinos de Finca at Pieros, from old vines on the clay slopes by the pilgrims' road. Aged about a year in French oak, it is round, ripe and supple, a red to pour beside roast meats or a stew.
records.story: Losada Vinos de Finca began in the middle of the 2000s, in 2004 or 2005 by different accounts, with the purchase of small plots of old Mencía around Pieros, a hamlet on the pilgrims' road between Cacabelos and Villafranca del Bierzo. Its idea was to recover old vineyards on the clay soils where the valley's growers had long planted Mencía, worked as many small plots rather than one estate. The namesake Losada is drawn from the clay slopes close to the cellar. Above it the range climbs to Altos de Losada, from old plots at Valtuille de Arriba aged in concrete eggs, large casks and barrels, and to La Bienquerida, a single plot of old mixed vines at Las Chas. From 2017, by its own account, the house farmed with cover crops between the rows and replanted with grafted Mencía. Bierzo is often taught through its slate, and Losada is the other half of the lesson. For a sommelier, the namesake wine is the softer side of Mencía: round and generous from clay, beside the taut reds of the slate hills, and an easy first bottle of the valley at the table.

questions.exp: Losada's old vines grow on the clay slopes near the cellar at Pieros, which the house holds gives a rounder Mencía; like the Corullón reds it is Mencía, not a Tempranillo blend.

The plan's note is answered: founded is left empty because Enterwine, Spanish Wine Lover and an interview of 2011 give 2005 and Wine Spies and another listing 2004, and the story gives both; the label is Losada with Bierzo on the house's page.

La Bienquerida's Vino de Paraje of Las Chas from 2018 rests on Bodeboca alone (in two languages), and no page of the Consejo read names it, so the record calls it a single plot at Las Chas and gives no rank; Bodeboca's planting of 1906 on slate and Enterwine's Las Chas at Valtuille de Abajo against the house's distributor's Valtuille de Arriba are left out.

The house's product page gives twelve months in French oak barrels for Losada and its Guía Gourmets notice of 2025 twelve months between concrete eggs and barrels with a touch of Doña Blanca; the record follows the product page, and the notice is not listed because its title carries a judgement.

Left out for want of a second source: the cellar opposite the hill of Castro Ventosa and its year (about 2009 by Alimarket), the shared shareholders and management with Bodegas Valdesil of Valdeorras by Alimarket in 2009, the local word piezas for the plots and the founders' story of a prophecy fulfilled (Enterwine alone).

Living names met, for people.json: the winemaker named on the house's page and in an interview address (Amancio Fernández Gómez) and the architect of the cellar (Jesús Manzanares, status not read, as a precaution); the house's page on the winemaker's training is not used because it would describe a present role.
